items.title: 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra
items.note: Watch this before writing a single line of lesson 1.1. It gives you the picture — vectors as arrows, matrices as movements — that the code then makes real.

items.title: 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Calculus
items.note: The derivative as a thing you can see rather than a rule you memorise. Everything in phase 1 about slopes and gradients assumes this picture.

items.title: 3Blue1Brown, Neural Networks (includes an outstanding attention/transformer series)
items.note: The clearest account of backpropagation anywhere, and the attention series at the end is the best transformer explainer that exists.

items.title: StatQuest with Josh Starmer
items.note: Short, cheerful, and relentlessly concrete. When a classical-ML idea refuses to land, there is almost always a StatQuest that fixes it in ten minutes.

items.title: Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
items.note: Builds autograd, then a language model, from nothing, live, with every mistake left in. The closest thing to this curriculum's method on video.

items.title: Dive into Deep Learning
items.note: A full textbook where every equation is followed by the code that runs it. The reference to reach for when you want depth on a specific method.

items.title: Jay Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer
items.note: The diagrams most people picture when they think about transformers. Read it before the paper, not after.

items.title: The Annotated Transformer, Harvard NLP
items.note: The Attention Is All You Need paper, line by line, with working code beside each paragraph. Read it once you can already write a small model.

items.title: Sebastian Raschka's blog
items.note: Careful, current writing on how LLMs actually work, with the benchmarks and caveats other posts leave out.

items.title: Distill.pub
items.note: Interactive papers you can poke at. No longer publishing, but what is there is still the high-water mark for explaining a method visually.

items.title: Chris Olah's blog
items.note: The LSTM and embedding posts are ten years old and still the best first explanation of either. Start with Understanding LSTMs.

items.title: Deep Learning, Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville
items.note: The standard reference. Dense, and not a first read — but when you need the formal statement of something, it is here and it is free.

items.title: MLU-Explain, Amazon's Machine Learning University
items.note: Short visual essays on the ideas that are easy to nod along to and hard to actually hold: bias-variance, cross-validation, ROC.

items.title: Sebastian Raschka, Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)
items.note: Builds a GPT end to end in PyTorch, one component per chapter. The natural sequel to this curriculum's phase 4.

items.title: Vizuara, Building LLMs from Scratch
items.note: Long-form walkthroughs of LLM internals, worked slowly enough to follow along by typing rather than watching.

items.title: Chip Huyen, AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models (2025)
items.note: What changes when a model becomes a product: evaluation, cost, latency, failure modes. Phase 5 territory, and the notebooks are open.

items.title: jamwithai/production-agentic-rag-course
items.note: A working retrieval-augmented agent rather than a toy demo, with the retrieval and evaluation parts taken seriously.

items.title: FareedKhan-dev/all-agentic-architectures
items.note: A catalogue of agent patterns implemented side by side, useful for seeing what the choices actually are before picking one.

items.title: Kaggle Learn and competitions
items.note: Where you find out whether it transfers. The micro-courses are thin; the competitions and public notebooks are the real material.

items.title: Papers with Code
items.note: A paper with the implementation attached. The fastest route from 'I read about this' to 'I ran this'.

items.title: Andrew Ng, Machine Learning Specialization (DeepLearning.AI)
items.note: The canonical first course. Our phase 2 covers the same ground by building it instead — useful as a second angle, not a substitute.

items.title: NPTEL, Artificial Intelligence: Search Methods for Problem Solving — Prof. Deepak Khemani, IIT Madras
items.note: Classical AI: search, heuristics, planning. Not on the path to a neural network, and worth knowing anyway — it is the half of AI that predates it.

items.title: Keith Galli, Complete Python NumPy Tutorial
items.note: One sitting, and lesson 1.1 stops being about NumPy syntax and starts being about vectors. Watch it first if you have never used arrays.
